name: Matera
title: Holidays in Matera
intro: Whole neighbourhoods of cave houses carved into a gorge, glowing with lights at night. Here's what Matera is like, when to go and how long to stay.
image_alt: The old cave town of Matera lit up at dusk, with a church tower in front
facts_note: The EU is bringing in new entry checks, so check the rules on GOV.UK before you book.
when_to_go: April, May, September and October are warm enough for exploring but cool enough for all the steps. July and August are very hot, so explore early and late. Winter is cold and quiet, but the Sassi look magical at Christmas. Easter and the Festa della Bruna on 2 July are busy, so book ahead for those.

things.name: Sassi di Matera
things.blurb: Wander the two old cave districts, Sasso Caveoso and Sasso Barisano. Expect lots of steps.

things.name: Casa Grotta di Vico Solitario
things.blurb: A furnished cave house showing how families and their animals once lived together.

things.name: Palombaro Lungo
things.blurb: A huge underground water tank under the main square, seen from walkways.

things.name: Santa Maria de Idris
things.blurb: A small church carved into a rock pinnacle, with old frescoes inside.

things.name: Belvedere di Murgia Timone
things.blurb: Walk across the gorge for the best view back to the town, past cave churches.

things.name: Alberobello
things.blurb: A town of white cone-roofed trulli houses, about an hour's drive away.

faqs.question: What is the best time to visit Matera?
faqs.answer: April, May, September and October, when it's around 18 to 26°C, warm enough for exploring but cool enough for all the steps. July and August are very hot, often above 30°C.

faqs.question: Is Matera worth visiting at Christmas?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you don't mind the cold. The Sassi are lit up and quiet, and there's often a living nativity among the cave houses on some December weekends. Check this year's dates before you book.

faqs.question: How many days do you need in Matera?
faqs.answer: Two or three days. One day covers the main sights of the Sassi; a second lets you walk across the gorge to the Murgia viewpoint and visit a cave church or two.

faqs.question: Is Matera worth visiting?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Sassi, two old districts of cave houses carved into a gorge, are unlike anywhere else in Europe, and sleeping in a cave hotel is part of the fun. It isn't a beach place, so most people spend two or three nights here and the rest of the week in Puglia. Children love the caves too.

faqs.question: How many nights do you need?
faqs.answer: Two or three nights is enough to explore the Sassi and walk across the gorge.

faqs.question: How do you get there from the UK?
faqs.answer: Fly to Bari, then drive about an hour, or take a local train. Italy is in the EU, so British passport holders can visit for up to 90 days in any 180 without a visa. New EU entry checks are being brought in, so check GOV.UK before you travel.

faqs.question: Can you visit Matera with a pushchair?
faqs.answer: Not easily. The Sassi are full of steep steps and uneven paths, so bring a baby carrier for little ones.

faqs.question: Can you combine Matera with Puglia?
faqs.answer: Easily. Matera is about an hour from Bari and from Alberobello, so many people spend a few nights in Matera and the rest of the week in Puglia, by the sea or among the trulli.

faqs.question: Where should you stay in Matera?
faqs.answer: In the Sassi, ideally in a cave hotel, so you can see the lights come on at night. Cars can't drive into most of the Sassi, so ask your hotel where to park or arrange a pick-up.
